articles.title: Making friends as an autistic adult
articles.summary: Part 1 of our friendship series: start from what you love, look for groups with a plan, try online spaces, bring a script and an exit line, and know that PEERS® runs in Canada.
articles.body_markdown:
*Part 1 of our friendship series. Part 2 is "Keeping friendships going".*

There's no single right way to make friends. Some people want a big circle; others want one or two people who get them. Both are fine. Here are some places to start.

## Start from what you love

Shared interests do a lot of the work. The National Autistic Society, a UK charity, points out that common ground makes it easier to start a conversation and keep it going. A game, a hobby, a fandom or a cause gives you something to talk about, and something to do while you talk.

## Look for structure

Clubs and regular activities come with a plan: a time, a place and a thing to do. That can make the social part feel lighter.

- In Toronto, the Geneva Centre for Autism runs a monthly Adult Social Club for neurodivergent adults, in person and online, for $20 a session.
- Autism Ontario's regional teams post events too. This fall, its Windsor team is running a Dungeons and Dragons night for autistic adults, open to all experience levels.
- Groups that aren't autism-specific count too: a board game café, a choir, a walking group or a class at a local college.

## Try online spaces

If you'd rather write than talk, online communities can be a gentle way in. The National Autistic Society runs forums just for autistic people, and many online groups are built around a single interest.

## Bring a script, and plan your exit

It's okay to prepare. The National Autistic Society suggests having a few questions or introductions ready, going along as an observer at first, and not feeling you have to stay for the whole session. "I'm heading off, see you next time" is a complete goodbye.

## Programs that teach friendship skills

Some people like learning the unwritten rules directly. PEERS® was first developed at UCLA and has been widely researched.

- **Ontario:** Kerry's Place offers PEERS® for Young Adults to autistic adults aged 18 to 35. It runs for 16 weeks, in person or online, and a parent or family member joins separate sessions as a social coach. It costs $2000 and is an eligible expense under Passport Funding.
- **Alberta:** the University of Calgary runs PEERS® for Young Adults for ages 19 to 28, at $1250, and some people can get a bursary.

These programs are one option among many. Plenty of people find their people without one.

### Where to start

- Pick one interest and find one group built around it.
- Save two opening lines and one exit line in your phone.
- Look through ResourceHub's social clubs and support groups.
- Curious about PEERS®? Ask Kerry's Place or the University of Calgary when the next group starts.

articles.title: Keeping friendships going
articles.summary: Part 2 of our friendship series: low-pressure ways to stay in touch, how to tell friends what works for you, what to do after a misunderstanding, and why a few good friends is plenty.
articles.body_markdown:
*Part 2 of our friendship series, after "Making friends as an autistic adult".*

Making a friend is one step. Staying in touch is another, and it can happen in ways that suit you.

## Keep it low-pressure

Staying close doesn't have to mean long calls or big plans. Small things count:

- Send a photo, a link or a meme about something you both like.
- Do something side by side: play a game online, watch the same show, go for a walk.
- Keep a standing plan, like the first Saturday of the month at the same café, so nobody has to organize it each time.

The National Autistic Society, a UK charity, suggests planning in times to see friends, even with a schedule for your week. A calendar reminder to check in with someone isn't fake. It's care.

## Say what works for you

Friends can't guess, and most would rather know. A short message can do a lot:

- "I'm better at texting than calls."
- "I sometimes take a day or two to reply. It doesn't mean I'm upset."
- "Somewhere quieter would help me enjoy it more."

Telling friends you're autistic is your choice. The National Autistic Society says it's up to you, and that it can help people understand what you need.

## When something goes wrong

Misunderstandings happen in every friendship. The researcher Damian Milton describes a "double empathy problem": when people with very different experiences of the world interact, both sides can find it hard to understand each other. So a mix-up isn't one person's fault.

If someone seems upset, it doesn't mean they don't like you. The National Autistic Society notes that saying sorry usually helps, and that if you're not sure what happened, you can ask. Writing it down can feel easier: "I think I upset you on Saturday. I'd like to understand what happened." It's okay to take some time before you reply.

## Quality over quantity

There's no right or wrong way to socialize, as the National Autistic Society puts it. One or two friends who accept you as you are can mean more than a big group. Friendships change too: some fade, some come back, and online friends are real friends.

### Where to start

- Send one friend something small this week.
- Write a short "how I keep in touch" note you can share.
- Set a gentle, repeating reminder to check in.
- Find a regular group in ResourceHub's social clubs and support groups.

articles.title: Finding your people: social and peer groups
articles.summary: Peer support groups, social clubs, skills programs like PEERS®, campus groups and online spaces: what each kind of group looks like for neurodivergent teens and adults, with Canadian examples and how to try one.
articles.body_markdown:
Spending time with people who get it can make a real difference. Groups for autistic, ADHD and other neurodivergent teens and adults come in a few kinds. Here's what each looks like, a few examples, and how to try one.

## Peer support groups

These are for talking and swapping strategies with people who've been there, often led by people with lived experience.

- CADDAC, a national ADHD charity, runs free monthly support groups on Zoom, led by trained facilitators who are adults with ADHD. There's also a free virtual group for ages 16 to 24.
- The Learning Disabilities Association of Toronto runs a free online group, every other week, for adults who have or think they have a learning disability or ADHD.

## Social and activity groups

These are built around doing something together, so the talking can come second. Autism organizations often post them as short series. This fall, for example, Autism Ontario is running a six-week run/walk club in Toronto for autistic teens and adults aged 16 and up, with no running experience needed.

## Skills programs

Some groups teach social skills directly, with practice built in.

- PEERS® was first developed at UCLA. In Canada, the University of Calgary runs it for teens aged 13 to 18, and Nova Scotia includes it in some specialized programming for junior and senior high students.
- The Learning Disabilities Association of Toronto's Befriend is a six-week Saturday group in North York for teens aged 14 to 18 with learning disabilities and/or ADHD.

Skills programs suit some people and not others. It's your call.

## Campus groups

Many colleges and universities have groups for neurodivergent students. At the University of Toronto, the Social Association for Students with ASD is for students who are diagnosed or who self-identify as autistic. Queen's University's Autism Group doesn't ask for documentation, a diagnosis or a referral.

## Online groups

If you'd rather write than talk, or there's nothing nearby, online groups built around one interest can be an easy first step.

## How to try one

- **Check who it's for:** age, location, online or in person, and whether you need a diagnosis. Some don't.
- **Ask what a session looks like.** The National Autistic Society, a UK charity, suggests getting in touch with the group leader to ask about the format, and checking whether there's a fee or a membership.
- **Ask if you can bring someone.** It also suggests asking whether a family member, friend or carer can come along.
- **Expect a first conversation.** Some groups start with an intake call or interview, like the Learning Disabilities Association of Toronto's. It's a good time to ask your own questions.
- **Give it two or three tries.** First sessions are often the hardest. If it still doesn't feel right, try a different kind of group.

### Where to start

- Pick the kind of group that sounds most like you.
- Write down two questions to ask the organizer.
- Look through ResourceHub's social clubs, support groups and campus pages.

articles.title: Ontario's autism program wait, compared with other provinces
articles.summary: How the Ontario Autism Program works, what official numbers say about the wait for core clinical services, and how BC, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Quebec and Nova Scotia fund autism support instead.
articles.body_markdown:
If you're waiting for Ontario's autism services, you may wonder how other provinces do it. Here's what official sources say. The first three sections are about Ontario only. Other provinces come after. Every amount here can change, so check the source pages before you plan around a number.

## How the Ontario Autism Program works (Ontario only)

The Ontario Autism Program (OAP) is for children and youth with a written autism diagnosis from a qualified professional, until age 18. You register through AccessOAP, the program's independent intake organization.

Some support is open once you're registered:

- Foundational family services, for everyone registered.
- Caregiver-mediated early years programs for children aged 12 to 48 months, and an entry to school program for children starting kindergarten or Grade 1. Ontario says eligible families with young children are invited to these when they register.
- Urgent response services, if your child or youth has an urgent need.

## The wait is for core clinical services (Ontario only)

Most of the waiting is for core clinical services: applied behaviour analysis, speech-language pathology, occupational therapy and mental health services. Children and youth are invited in the order they registered, as the program's advisory panel recommended.

After you accept an invitation, an AccessOAP care coordinator works with you to find your child's level of support needs (limited, moderate or extensive) for their age. Yearly funding ranges from $6,600 to $65,000.

If you registered by March 31, 2021, you may be eligible for interim one-time funding while you wait: $22,000 for a child under 6, or $5,500 for ages 6 to 17, based on age on April 1, 2026. Taking it doesn't change your child's place in line for core clinical services.

## What the official numbers say (Ontario only)

- Ontario's Financial Accountability Office (FAO) reported in June 2024 that 70,176 children were registered in the OAP by the end of 2023–24. As of February 29, 2024, 19,966 had been enrolled in core clinical services.
- The Ontario government says that by March 2025, 22,000 children and youth were actively enrolled in core clinical services. It added $120 million to the OAP in 2024–25.
- The province committed to a $600 million yearly budget in 2019. The FAO estimated that, at the 2023–24 average, $600 million a year would fully fund core clinical services for about 10,142 children and youth.

We didn't find an official average wait time for core clinical services. Because invitations go by registration date, registering soon after you get a written diagnosis means your place in line starts sooner.

## How some other provinces do it

Each province sets up autism support its own way. A few examples:

- **British Columbia** gives up to $22,000 a year for children under 6, and up to $6,000 a year for ages 6 to 18. This is changing: Autism Funding takes new applications until March 2027 and ends on March 31, 2027. A new B.C. Children and Youth Disability Benefit, for children with significant disabilities, will pay $6,500 or $17,000 a year, based on need. From July 2027, an income-tested supplement will offer up to $6,000 a year to families of children eligible for the federal disability tax credit.
- **Alberta's** Family Support for Children with Disabilities (FSCD) program works out supports with each family, based on the child's and family's needs. A child can qualify while awaiting a diagnosis. Children with severe disabilities may get specialized services from a team of health professionals.
- **Saskatchewan** gives up to $8,000 a year for children under 6, and up to $6,000 a year for ages 6 to 11. The Saskatchewan Health Authority also offers autism supports for children up to 19 with known or suspected autism.
- **Quebec** offers services for autistic people and people with disabilities, and for their families, after a needs assessment, with no fee or deductible. You start by contacting your territorial establishment.
- **Nova Scotia's** Provincial Preschool Autism Service offers needs-based services for preschool-age children and families across the province.

None of these provinces' pages gave a single wait time either, so the most useful question is a direct one: "What can we get now, and how long is the wait for the rest?"

## What's Ontario-only, and what changes

- The OAP, AccessOAP, core clinical services and interim one-time funding exist only in Ontario.
- If you move, expect to apply again. Saskatchewan, for example, has out-of-province diagnoses reviewed by the Saskatchewan Health Authority.
- Amounts, age bands and program names change. BC's program is changing now. Ontario's extra $120 million was a one-time investment, and the FAO assumed funding would go back to $600 million a year.

### Where to start

- In Ontario, register with AccessOAP as soon as you have a written diagnosis, and ask which services you can use now.
- Outside Ontario, start with your province's page and ask what's available before a diagnosis.
- Look through ResourceHub's funding help and support for parents.

articles.title: Siblings: a different kind of closeness
articles.summary: Growing up with a neurodivergent brother or sister can bring its own kind of closeness. Ways to connect, room for your own feelings, and sibling groups in Canada, from Sibshops to SibNet.
articles.body_markdown:
Growing up with an autistic or otherwise neurodivergent brother or sister can bring its own kind of closeness. It might be a show you always watch together, a game with your own rules, or sitting in the same room without needing to talk.

## Taking time

A lot of sibling closeness is patience: waiting for an answer, explaining plans before they happen, or saying things in fewer words. Some siblings write things down, use pictures, or learn how their brother or sister communicates best, whether that's speech, typing, signs or a device. The National Autistic Society, a UK charity, suggests including your sibling in family plans in whatever way of communicating gives them a say.

## Your own ways to connect

- Spend ten minutes on their favourite thing, on their terms.
- Make up a private joke, a handshake or a code word.
- Send each other videos or messages, even under the same roof.

## A strength you can name

The National Autistic Society notes that having an autistic sibling can be a positive experience, and may help you become a more accepting person. Patience and noticing what others need are skills many siblings carry into friendships and work.

## Your needs matter too

It's okay to feel proud, protective, frustrated or left out, sometimes all in one day. The National Autistic Society suggests telling your parents how you feel (by text or email, if that's easier) and asking for some time that's just you and them. Talking with other siblings can help too.

## Sibling groups

Sibshops give siblings of kids with disabilities peer support and information in a lively, recreational setting, and they're used across the United States and Canada. In a small University of Washington survey of 30 adults who went as children, over 90% said Sibshops had a positive effect on how they felt about their siblings.

Some options in Canada:

- **Holland Bloorview** (Toronto) runs a Sibling Support Program for ages 7 to 18, open to families who aren't hospital clients.
- **ErinoakKids** offers free monthly Sibshops through the school year for siblings of its clients, aged 4 to 18.
- **Autism Ontario's** Sib Squad is a multi-week group for siblings aged 7 to 12 who have an autistic brother or sister.
- **Community Options for Children and Families** in Victoria, BC runs Sibshops for ages 7 to 15.

Adult siblings can join SibNet, an online community from the Sibling Support Project.

### Where to start

- Ask a parent for some one-on-one time. A text works.
- Try one new way to connect with your sibling this week.
- Find a sibling group near you on ResourceHub.
- If you're an adult sibling, have a look at SibNet.

articles.notes: Written for siblings of any age, with a short line for adult siblings. Canadian options are Ontario (Holland Bloorview in Toronto; ErinoakKids in Brampton, Mississauga, Oakville and Orangeville; Autism Ontario's Sib Squad, here the London group, 5 to 26 November 2026, $10 a child, with others listed in Windsor and Niagara Falls) and BC (Community Options, Victoria). To check before publishing: (1) ErinoakKids' Sibshops are only for siblings of current ErinoakKids clients. (2) Holland Bloorview's program is, for now, for children who don't need personal, communication or equipment support themselves, and families are referred through a form. (3) The University of Washington figure is a small 2005 survey (30 adults) reported by the Sibling Support Project itself, so we call it small. (4) The NAS siblings guide was last reviewed 11 August 2020. (5) SibNet is a Facebook group for adult siblings only. ResourceHub's 'For siblings' search lists 21 checked sibling services, including these.
